questions.question: State what is meant by drift velocity of charge carriers.
questions.answer: Drift velocity is the average (net) velocity of the charge carriers in a conductor in the direction set by the electric field.
steps: Charge carriers in a metal move randomly at high speed, so their net motion is zero.
A potential difference sets up an electric field in the wire.
The field causes a small net movement of the carriers in one direction.
Drift velocity is the average velocity of this net movement; for electrons it is opposite to conventional current.

Take the electron charge q = 1.60 x 10^-19 C from the data booklet.

questions.question: The battery supplies a constant current while the skateboard is in use, delivering 36 000 C over 40 minutes. Find the number of electrons passing a point during the 0.45 s from part (b)(i).
questions.answer: Number of electrons = 4.2 x 10^19
steps: Constant current I = Q / t = 36 000 C / (40 x 60 s) = 15 A.
Charge passing in 0.45 s: Q = I t = 15 A x 0.45 s = 6.75 C.
Number of electrons N = Q / e = 6.75 C / 1.60 x 10^-19 C.
N = 4.2 x 10^19 electrons.

questions.question: A student plans to find the resistivity of a metal wire graphically. State the physical quantities to measure and a suitable instrument for each.
questions.answer: Length with a metre rule; diameter with a micrometer screw gauge; potential difference with a voltmeter and current with an ammeter (giving resistance).
steps: Resistivity rho = R A / L, so the quantities needed are R, A (from diameter) and L.
Length L: measure along the wire with a metre rule or tape measure.
Diameter d: measure with a micrometer screw gauge at several points; A = pi d^2 / 4.
Resistance R: measure the current with an ammeter in series and the pd with a voltmeter across the wire; R = V / I.

questions.question: Describe how her measurements can give an accurate value of resistivity using a graph.
questions.answer: Plot R against L; the gradient g gives rho = g x A, where A = pi d^2 / 4.
steps: Measure R for several different lengths L of wire, keeping the diameter the same.
Plot R (y-axis) against L (x-axis); R is proportional to L, so the line passes through the origin.
Draw a line of best fit and find its gradient g = rho / A.
Use the mean diameter to find A = pi d^2 / 4, then calculate rho = g x A.
Using a gradient from many points reduces the effect of random errors.

questions.question: Two copper wires of identical cross-sectional area are in series. Which quantity could be different for the two wires? A charge carrier density, B current, C drift velocity, D potential difference.
questions.answer: D - potential difference
steps: In series the current is the same in both wires, so B is the same.
Both wires are copper (same n) with the same area A, so v = I / (nqA) is the same: C is the same.
Charge carrier density is the same for copper: A is the same.
Potential difference V = I R depends on each wire's resistance, which depends on length, so D can differ.

questions.question: State what is meant by the work function of a metal.
questions.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal.
steps: Electrons in a metal need energy to escape from its surface.
The work function phi is the least energy needed to remove an electron from the surface.
Electrons at lower energy levels in the metal need more energy than the work function to escape.
Answer: the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface.

questions.question: A photocell works with ultraviolet light but not with visible light. Explain why.
questions.answer: Photon energy hf of UV exceeds the work function; visible light photons have energy below the work function.
steps: Photoemission happens only if a single photon has energy hf at least equal to the work function phi.
Ultraviolet photons have a higher frequency, so more energy per photon, than visible photons.
Visible light frequencies are below the threshold frequency f0 = phi / h for this metal.
So visible photons cannot eject electrons, while UV photons can.

questions.question: With 0 V applied, the ammeter reads 2.4 A. The UV intensity is increased at constant frequency. Explain what happens to the ammeter reading.
questions.answer: The ammeter reading increases: more photons per second each eject an electron, so more electrons pass per second.
steps: Intensity is the power per unit area, so higher intensity means more photons arrive per second.
Frequency is unchanged, so each photon has the same energy and can eject one electron if it exceeds the work function.
More photons per second means more photoelectrons are emitted per second.
Current is charge per second, so the ammeter reading rises above 2.4 A; the maximum kinetic energy of electrons does not change.

questions.question: The pd is adjusted until the ammeter reads zero; the voltmeter reads 3.59 V. The UV frequency is 2.00 x 10^15 Hz. Calculate the work function in joules.
questions.answer: Work function = 7.5 x 10^-19 J
steps: At zero current the stopping pd gives the maximum kinetic energy: Ek = e V = 1.60 x 10^-19 C x 3.59 V = 5.74 x 10^-19 J.
Photon energy E = h f = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s x 2.00 x 10^15 Hz = 1.33 x 10^-18 J.
Einstein's equation: hf = phi + Ek, so phi = hf - Ek.

questions.question: Which statement about physical quantities or units is correct? A current is derived; B power is derived; C the coulomb is a base unit; D the volt is a base unit.
questions.answer: B - power is a derived quantity
steps: Current is a base quantity (ampere), so A is wrong.
Power = energy / time is built from base quantities, so it is derived: B is correct.
The coulomb = ampere x second is a derived unit, so C is wrong.
The volt = J C^-1 is a derived unit, so D is wrong. Answer: B.

questions.question: State the purpose of the resistor in the circuit with wires W and Z in series with a cell.
questions.answer: To limit (control) the current in the circuit.

By Ohm's law the current I = V / R_total is kept at a controlled, safe value.
This protects the cell and the wires from an excessive current.

questions.question: Equal lengths of copper wires W and Z, with Z having twice the diameter of W, are in parallel. Explain why the drift velocity of the charge carriers is the same in both.
questions.answer: Both have the same pd and length, so R is proportional to 1/A. Z has 4x the area and 4x the current, so v = I / (nqA) is the same.

Drift velocity v = I / (nqA): both current and area are x4, so v is the same in both wires.

For diffraction d sin theta = lambda, so the angle theta decreases.

questions.question: Explain why a current is detected with UV light on magnesium and copper gauze, and why the current falls to zero when the power supply polarity is reversed.
questions.answer: UV photons eject photoelectrons from the magnesium; with the gauze positive they are attracted across the gap, giving a current. Reversing the supply repels them, so the current stops.
steps: UV photons with energy above the work function of magnesium eject photoelectrons from the ribbon.
With the gauze positive and the ribbon negative, the photoelectrons are attracted across the air gap to the gauze.
This flow of electrons (charge) is detected as a current by the ammeter.
When the supply is reversed, the gauze is negative, so the photoelectrons are repelled back to the ribbon.
No electrons reach the gauze, so the current falls to zero.
The result shows that light is absorbed as photons and electrons are emitted only when each photon has enough energy.

steps: Greater intensity means more photons per second strike the ribbon.
The frequency is unchanged, so each photon has the same energy and the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is unchanged.
More photons give more photoelectrons emitted per second.
So the current measured by the ammeter increases.

questions.question: A laser emitting red light of wavelength 633 nm replaces the UV lamp. The work function of magnesium is 3.7 eV. Deduce whether the photoelectric effect occurs.

steps: Convert to electronvolts: 3.14 x 10^-19 J / 1.60 x 10^-19 J per eV = 1.96 eV.
The work function is 3.7 eV, which is greater than the photon energy.
A single photon cannot release an electron, so the photoelectric effect does not occur regardless of intensity.

questions.question: Explain how a large pd across a discharge tube causes the gas atoms to emit photons.
questions.answer: Electrons accelerated by the pd collide with gas atoms and excite them to higher energy levels; when they fall back, photons of fixed frequency (hf = difference in energy levels) are emitted.
steps: The large pd accelerates free electrons in the tube, giving them kinetic energy E = eV.
Accelerated electrons collide with gas atoms and transfer some kinetic energy to them.
If the energy transferred matches an energy gap, an atomic electron is excited to a higher energy level.
The excited electron is unstable and drops back to a lower energy level.
The energy lost in the drop is emitted as a photon, with hf = E2 - E1.
Because the energy levels are discrete, the photons have specific frequencies (a line spectrum).

questions.question: Photons of energy 4.75 eV are incident on a metal with work function 6.30 x 10^-19 J. Show the maximum speed of emitted electrons is about 5.3 x 10^5 m s^-1.

Ek = (1/2) m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 Ek / m) with m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg.

B and D describe charge and current, not an energy change.
Answer: C.

questions.question: A wire of length 0.25 m has resistance 65 (read as 65 milliohm, unit symbol lost in text) and resistivity 5.6 x 10^-8 ohm m. Calculate its diameter, assuming a circular cross-section.
questions.answer: Diameter = 0.52 mm
steps: Resistance R = rho L / A, so A = rho L / R.
For a circle A = pi d^2 / 4, so d = sqrt(4 A / pi).

questions.question: State what is meant by diffraction.
questions.answer: The spreading of waves when they pass through a gap or around an obstacle of similar size to their wavelength.
steps: Diffraction is the spreading out of a wave as it passes through a slit or around an edge.
The effect is greatest when the gap or obstacle size is comparable to the wavelength.
Electron diffraction by graphite shows that electrons have wave properties.
Answer: spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle of similar size to the wavelength.

questions.question: An electron is accelerated through 4.9 kV. Show that its de Broglie wavelength is about 1.8 x 10^-11 m.
questions.answer: lambda = 1.75 x 10^-11 m, which is about 1.8 x 10^-11 m.
steps: Kinetic energy gained: (1/2) m v^2 = e V, so momentum p = m v = sqrt(2 m e V).
This is about 1.8 x 10^-11 m, as shown.

questions.question: A grating with 5000 lines per cm is proposed for the electron beam, with the screen about 1 m away. Deduce whether a second-order maximum would be clearly visible, given lambda = 1.8 x 10^-11 m.
questions.answer: No. The maximum lies only about 0.018 mm from the centre, too close to be clearly seen.
steps: Grating spacing d = 1 / (5000 lines per cm) = 1 / (5.0 x 10^5 lines per m) = 2.0 x 10^-6 m.
Second order: d sin theta = 2 lambda, so sin theta = 2 x 1.8 x 10^-11 / 2.0 x 10^-6 = 1.8 x 10^-5.
Position on screen at 1 m: y = L tan theta, approximately 1 m x 1.8 x 10^-5 = 1.8 x 10^-5 m = 0.018 mm.
This separation is far too small to be seen clearly, so the second-order maximum would not be clearly visible.

questions.question: The formula I = nqvA is used for current in a conductor. Which gives the meaning of n? A conduction electrons in a wire of length 1 m; B conduction electrons in 1 m^3 of material; C total electrons in a wire of length 1 m; D total electrons in 1 m^3 of material.
questions.answer: B - number of conduction electrons in 1 m^3 of a material
steps: n in I = nqvA is the number density of charge carriers.
Number density is the number of carriers per unit volume, so it is per m^3.
Options A and C refer to a wire length, not a volume, so they are wrong.
Option D gives all electrons, not conduction electrons, so answer B.

questions.question: A solar lamp cell stores 6.0 kJ of energy and has a constant emf of 1.5 V. Which is the charge passing through the lamp when the cell discharges fully? A 0.25 C; B 4.0 C; C 4000 C; D 9000 C.
steps: Energy transferred by the cell E = Q V, where V is its emf.
Rearrange: Q = E / V = 6.0 x 10^3 J / 1.5 V.
Answer: C.

questions.question: Wires X and Y are in series and made of the same material. X has twice the diameter of Y and electrons in X have mean drift velocity v. What is the mean drift velocity in Y? A 0.25 v; B 0.5 v; C 2v; D 4v.
questions.answer: D - 4v
steps: The wires are in series, so the current I is the same in both.
Same material means n and q are the same.
v = I / (nqA), so v is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area A.
Wire X has 4 times the area of Y, so Y's drift velocity is 4 times v. Answer: D.

questions.question: Which unit is equivalent to the coulomb? A A s^-1; B J V^-1; C W A^-1; D W V^-1.
questions.answer: B - J V^-1
steps: Charge Q = I t, so the coulomb is the ampere second (A s).
Volt = J C^-1, so J V^-1 = J / (J C^-1) = C.
A s^-1 is not a charge; W A^-1 is the volt; W V^-1 is the ampere.
Answer: B.

questions.question: A monochromatic beam with all photons of the same energy produces photoelectrons with a range of kinetic energies. Explain why.
questions.answer: Electrons come from different depths in the metal and lose different amounts of energy in collisions before escaping, so the kinetic energies range from 0 up to hf - phi.
steps: Every photon has the same energy hf.
An electron at the surface needs only the work function phi, so it leaves with the maximum Ek = hf - phi.
Electrons deeper in the metal lose energy in collisions before reaching the surface, so they leave with less kinetic energy.
So emitted electrons have kinetic energies from zero up to hf - phi.

questions.question: Explain what the observations (white light at low and high intensity gives no current; UV at low intensity gives a current) show about the nature of light.
questions.answer: Light is made of photons; emission depends on the photon frequency (energy) rather than intensity, so UV photons above the work function release electrons while visible photons do not.
steps: Light carries energy in discrete packets called photons, each with energy hf.
An electron is emitted only if one photon has energy at least the work function.
White light contains only frequencies below the threshold, so no electrons are emitted at any intensity.
Ultraviolet photons have energy above the work function, so even low intensity gives emission (one photon, one electron).
Intensity only changes how many photons arrive per second, so it affects the number of electrons, not whether emission happens.
